Something is entrenched when it has become so deeply fixed, settled, or established — usually over a long period of time — that it is very difficult, or sometimes nearly impossible, to change, remove, or challenge.

The single most important idea in this word is resistance to change. Whatever is entrenched has "dug itself in" so deep that it isn't going anywhere easily.

A good mental image: think of a very old, very large tree. Its roots have spread wide and gone deep into the earth over decades. You can shake its branches all you want, but the tree itself will not move. That is exactly the feeling of "entrenched." Something has rooted itself so firmly that pushing back against it feels almost futile.

This adjective is flexible — it can describe many different kinds of things. Here are the most common:

Beliefs and attitudes. When a person has held a belief for so long that no argument, fact, or new experience seems to shake it, that belief is entrenched. For example: "He has entrenched views about how children should be raised, and nothing you say will change them." The belief isn't just strong — it has become almost a permanent part of how that person sees the world.

Habits and behaviors. A habit becomes entrenched when it has been repeated for so long that it feels automatic, natural, and deeply resistant to breaking. "Her entrenched routine of waking up at 5 AM survived even vacations and illness."

Systems and institutions. Organizations, governments, industries, and social structures can be entrenched when they have existed for so long and become so embedded in how things work that reforming or replacing them feels almost impossible. "The entrenched bureaucracy blocked every attempt at reform."

Power and privilege. When certain people or groups hold power for so long that their position feels untouchable, they are entrenched. "The entrenched ruling class resisted every movement for democratic change."

Problems and inequalities. Even negative things — poverty, discrimination, corruption — can be entrenched when they have been present so long and run so deep that solving them becomes extraordinarily difficult. "Generations of entrenched poverty made it hard for families in that region to break the cycle."

"Entrenched" almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When someone calls something entrenched, they are usually suggesting that it should be changed or challenged, but that it stubbornly refuses to be. There is a sense of frustration baked into the word — the feeling that something old and immovable is standing in the way of progress or improvement.

However, it can occasionally be used in a neutral or even slightly positive sense — for example, describing deep-rooted traditions or values that a community is proud of. But this is less common. In most real-world usage, if someone calls something entrenched, they are pointing to it as a problem.

Not everything fixed or established is entrenched. The word implies an extreme degree of being rooted. A habit you've had for two weeks is not entrenched. A prejudice someone has held since childhood, reinforced over fifty years, and defended against every challenge — that is entrenched. The word signals that something has gone far beyond ordinary stubbornness or stability. It has reached a level where change would require enormous effort, time, or force — and might still fail.

It is important not to confuse "entrenched" with simply "strong" or "common."

Something can be strong but still flexible and open to change — that is not entrenched. Something can be common or widespread but still shift over time — that is not entrenched either.

"Entrenched" specifically means the thing has settled in so deeply that it actively resists being moved. The resistance and the difficulty of change are the heart of the word.
How It Looks in a Sentence

The word almost always appears right before the noun it describes, or after linking verbs like "is," "remain," or "become."

  • "Entrenched inequality makes social mobility very hard."
  • "These attitudes are deeply entrenched in the culture."
  • "The problem has become so entrenched that a quick fix is impossible."
  • "They are fighting against an entrenched system."

You will also very frequently see it paired with the adverb "deeply" — as in "deeply entrenched" — to emphasize just how fixed something is.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: entrenched = so deeply fixed that change is extremely hard or nearly impossible. It describes things — beliefs, habits, systems, power, problems — that have dug themselves in so thoroughly over time that they won't budge without enormous effort, if they move at all.
